conservation.notes: Globally near threatened and listed as vulnerable at Australian national level, and endangered under the New South Wales Threatened Species Conservation Act 1995; it has disappeared from an estimated 90% of its former Australian range. In New Zealand the contrast is complete: the frogs are abundant, and are classified there as feral and unprotected.

human_tolerance.notes: Most often found in areas affected by human habitation, including former industrial sites such as the Brickpit at Sydney Olympic Park, disused land and even human vessels such as bathtubs, and it prefers water bodies with emergent vegetation in and around built-up places.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Breeds in the warmer months from October to March, although some cases have been recorded earlier at the end of winter; more southerly and highland populations have a shorter window than northerly and lowland ones. Males call, usually while floating in the water and sometimes from vegetation at the side of a pond, mainly at night, and respond to recordings so that whole groups call in unison. Amplexus takes between ten minutes and five days in the wild, and an average of 5,000 eggs are deposited amongst aquatic vegetation in a gelatinous mass, with one recorded clump of 11,682; AmphiBIO independently records 1,960-11,682 eggs with one reproductive output a year. AmphiBIO also records size at maturity of 50-65 mm, matching the article's 45-50 mm for males and 65 mm for females.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: The frogs are much less active through the cool months, except in warmer or wetter periods, and darken almost to black in the cold. Winter habitat consists of whatever shelter is available around the breeding site, which can be vegetation, rocks, rubbish, or human debris and discarded building materials.

vocalizations.description: A deep growl, described as a four-part walk-walk sound and likened to the noise of a motorbike changing gears. Males call while floating in the water, sometimes from vegetation at the pond edge, and calling is more likely immediately after rain and within a narrow temperature band.

taxonomy.note: GBIF backbone gives Ranoidea aurea (Lesson, 1829) in Pelodryadidae, order Anura, class Amphibia. The article records a long nomenclatural history under Rana, Hyla, Litoria and Ranoidea and places the species in the Ranoidea aurea complex. AmphiBIO still files the species under Litoria aurea in the family Hylidae, the placement the article describes as the reason it was moved out of Ranidae; Pelodryadidae is the currently accepted family in the GBIF backbone and is used here. Note that the article's Taxonomy prose says Lesson described it in 1827 while both the GBIF backbone and the article's own infobox give 1829, and the backbone date is followed here.

external.note: GBIF usage key 10595763 matches the backbone and carries the full synonymy (Hyla aurea, Litoria aurea, Rana aurea, Ranoidea jacksoniensis, Ranoidea resplendens and others). ITIS TSN 662862 comes from Wikidata P815 and NCBI 8371 from Wikidata P685; NCBI Taxonomy independently returns Ranoidea aurea at 8371, confirming the identifier. The iNaturalist id needed care: Wikidata's P3151 points at 23572, which is iNaturalist's deprecated and now empty Litoria aurea concept, so inat_taxon_id is 517069 instead, iNaturalist's active Ranoidea aurea taxon with the same English name and the same English Wikipedia article.

common_names.note: Wikidata P1843 gives the English names (Green and golden bell frog, Golden Bell Frog, Green and Golden Bell Frog, Green and Golden Swamp Frog, Green Frog) and the Dutch gouden boomkikker; no French or German name is recorded, so none is asserted. The article adds green bell frog and records that the common name was first adopted by Harold Cogger in 1975, before which the bird was called the golden frog and golden tree frog. GBIF's vernacular names for the same key carry the Catalogue of Life and TAXREF spellings.

conservation.note: The article's infobox gives the IUCN status as NT and cites IUCN taxon e.T12143A3325402; Wikidata's P141 carries two values, of which the preferred rank is near threatened and the normal-rank value is vulnerable. NT is used here. The article's Conservation status prose, describing the older Australian listings, calls it globally and nationally vulnerable and records that in contrast to Australia the frogs are abundant in New Zealand and classified as feral and unprotected. The IUCN Red List pages themselves are not openly licensed, so the status is taken from the article's infobox and Wikidata rather than read from IUCN directly.

range.note: Distribution section: native to south-eastern Australia, historically from Brunswick Heads in northern New South Wales to East Gippsland in Victoria and west to Bathurst, Tumut and the ACT; 'It was introduced to New Zealand in the 1860s by the Auckland Acclimation Society, and it is now common in the part of the North Island north of Rotorua, and can also be found in South Taranaki and some isolated areas of Southland near Te Anau'; also introduced to New Caledonia and Vanuatu in the 19th century and common there. New Caledonia is carried as the ISO 3166-2 subdivision FR-NC because no alpha-2 code exists for it. Three offshore Australian islands (Kooragang, Broughton and Bowen) have no ISO codes and are recorded here rather than in the country list. The New Zealand and Vanuatu populations are feral, which is why NZ is also listed under invasive_in.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Ecology section: 'it spends most of its time within 10 cm of the ground and rarely ventures more than a metre above the ground', hopping between basking places, and the species is usually found in water bodies. AmphiBIO flags the species as terrestrial, aquatic and arboreal. Hop, walk and swim are therefore the three gaits, with only a token arboreal component. Climb is not included: the article says explicitly that 'the frog does not choose to climb trees or live up them to any significant extent'.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Ecology section: it 'spends much time basking in the sun' and 'is often active during the day ... mainly to warm in the sun', which is ectothermy stated plainly.

traits.skin.note: Ecology section: when handled the species 'secretes a slimy acrid mucus'.

traits.metamorphosis.note: Diet and predators section describes free-living tadpoles that feed on detritus, algae and bacteria, and AmphiBIO flags the species as larval (Lar = 1), direct development absent (Dir = 0) and viviparity absent (Viv = 0).

traits.perching.note: Ecology section: 'the frog does not choose to climb trees or live up them to any significant extent. It spends most of its time within 10 cm of the ground and rarely ventures more than a metre above the ground.' perching is therefore false and the block model carries no perched pose, even though AmphiBIO lists the species as arboreal in part.

traits.nest_type.note: Reproduction section: 'An average of 5,000 eggs are deposited amongst aquatic vegetation in a gelatinous mass'. No nest is built, so None is the matching nest type; the eggs are carried as a pond Nesting resource instead.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: 0.05 kg falls in the Small band (Tiny is strictly under 0.05 kg).

traits.mass_kg.note: AmphiBIO Body_mass_g = 50, for Litoria aurea, which is this species under its former genus combination. The article gives length but no weight. mass_range_kg was left unset because neither source gives a weight range.

traits.length_m.note: Wikipedia: 'adults range from 4.5 to 11 cm in length; typical specimens measure 6 to 8 cm', so the midpoint of the typical range, 7 cm, is used. AmphiBIO independently gives Body_size_mm = 93.9, near the top of the article's adult range.

traits.lifespan_y.note: AmphiBIO Longevity_max_y = 10. That is a maximum, not a mean, and the article states no lifespan at all, so this is an upper bound used directly as the trait value; treat it as the longest life recorded rather than a typical one.

traits.diet.note: Diet and predators section gives a long invertebrate list (crickets, larvae, mosquito wrigglers, dragonflies, earthworms, cockroaches, flies, grasshoppers, freshwater crayfish, slugs and, in captivity, spiders, molluscs and even mice) plus other frogs including their own species, and states outright that 'the relative proportion that various prey make up in the frog's diet is not known'. The shares are therefore derived rather than measured: invertebrate 0.85, vertebrate 0.15, reflecting a predominantly invertebrate diet with regular but secondary cannibalism and frog-taking. AmphiBIO independently flags arthropods (Arthro = 1).

traits.social.note: Ecology section records males fighting one another when they come within a metre of each other, and males responding to recordings so that groups call in unison, but neither is a stable group. Solitary with group_size 1-1 reflects that the animal is normally encountered alone at a breeding site.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Ecology section: 'Unlike most frog species, it is often active during the day', and the diurnal activity is mostly for basking in the sun. AmphiBIO flags Diu = 1 (and also Noc = 1, which the article's 'males call ... mainly at night' accounts for). Diurnal is used because basking and foraging dominate; the nocturnal component is carried by the call's time_windows rather than by duplicating it here.

traits.defense.note: Ecology section: when handled the species secretes a slimy acrid mucus made of 17 aurein peptides, which 'makes the frog slippery and hard to grip, and is poisonous to some other species of frogs, so it is a useful defensive tool'. Toxin is the matching defense; the schema's enum has no autotomy-like entry, and a defensive secretion is what this is.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.2. The frog is described as tolerant of people to the point of being found in human vessels such as bathtubs, living in disused industrial land and former brick pits, and it 'has the ability to sit still for several hours'.

habitat.use.note: Ecology section: basking on vegetation, rocks and reeds usually near water or hopping between such places; 'It spends most of its time within 10 cm of the ground and rarely ventures more than a metre above the ground'; usually found in still, shallow, unshaded freshwater ponds. AmphiBIO flags Ter = 1, Aqu = 1 and Arb = 1. ground 0.6 / aquatic 0.3 / arboreal 0.1.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Ecology section: 'winter habitats consist of available shelters around the breeding site', and the frog prefers water bodies with emergent vegetation. pond is the matching shelter tag, since the refuge is the breeding water and its marginal cover rather than a burrow, litter or canopy.

habitat.resources.note: Diet and predators section for the prey; Ecology section for the still shallow water with emergent vegetation, the grassy terrestrial feeding grounds close at hand, and the winter cover around the breeding site; Reproduction section for the eggs deposited in aquatic vegetation. No monthly or seasonal weighting of the prey shares was applied because the article explicitly says the proportions are unknown.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Ecology section: 'it is most often found in areas that have been affected by human habitation', populations persist at former industrial sites such as the Brickpit at Sydney Olympic Park, and the frog 'has even been found in human vessels such as bathtubs'; Conservation status adds that in New Zealand it is abundant and unprotected. Exploiter is the matching affinity. impervious_max, light_max and flight_distance_m are authored judgements.

seasonal.strategy.note: The article describes a year-round resident that is less active only through the cool months and can be active in winter during warmer or wetter periods, with no migration or dormancy of several months: ActiveYearRound. The cool-month lull is carried as a phase.

seasonal.phases.note: Reproduction section for the October-March breeding season, the earlier cases at the end of winter, the shorter window in southerly and highland populations, night calling from water, the amplexus period and the roughly 5,000 eggs in a gelatinous mass among aquatic vegetation; Ecology section for the cool-month inactivity, the near-black cold-weather colouration and the winter shelters around the breeding site; AmphiBIO for the 1,960-11,682 egg range, the single annual reproductive output, the 50-65 mm size at maturity and the 0.5-1.6 year age at maturity. The end of the breeding phase (30 April) and the start of the dormancy phase (1 May) are authored judgements that close the gap the article leaves around the cited months, and both phases are restricted to NZ because the cited temperature, timing and reproductive observations come from Australian populations.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg, free-living tadpole, metamorphosed juvenile and adult are all explicitly described: eggs in a gelatinous mass, tadpoles feeding on detritus, algae and bacteria, recently metamorphosed individuals entering shallow water, and maturity at 9-12 months in males and two years in females. duration_days was left unset for every stage because no source consulted gives an incubation or tadpole duration, and guessing one would be dishonest.

vocalizations.growl.note: Reproduction section: males call 'with a deep growl that has been described as a four-part "walk-walk sound" - likened to the sound of a motorbike changing gears', usually while floating in the water and sometimes from vegetation at the side of a pond, mainly at night; males respond to recordings of the call, so entire groups will then call in unison.

look.note: Description section for the plumage-equivalent: a large stout frog, almost completely green from dark pea-green to bright emerald or marked with metallic brassy, dull copper-brown or gold, or almost completely bronze, with females tending to have more green than males; a creamy-white or pale yellow stripe bordered above with gold and below with black running from behind the eye across the copper tympanum to the groin and rising into a dorsolateral fold; a second stripe from below the eye to the shoulder; a cream or white coarsely granular abdomen; green, bronze or both legs with blue-green inner thighs and groins; enlarged toe discs, free fingers and almost completely webbed toes; and a pale gold vocal sac on mature males. Proportions are authored against the anuran body plan for a large frog with a pointed snout and long legs, and the dorsolateral stripe is carried as a mirrored extra part because it is the species' most recognisable marking. Colour variation is wide (including a near-black cold-weather form and occasional melanics), so the palette is the typical green-and-gold individual.

behavior.note: Authored bespoke program (fsm-bell-frog-v1) with authored parameters. A bespoke program is justified because none of the four shared programs fits: fsm-anuran-nocturnal-v1 is explicitly a nocturnal pond frog and inverts this species' day/night pattern (it gates its whole loop on is_day, hiding by day and emerging at night, whereas the article says this frog is often active during the day); fsm-ground-forager-v1 is written for a furred endothermic mammal with four-legged gaits and no basking or calling state; bt-perching-songbird-v1 assumes flight and perching; and fsm-seabird-predator-v1 assumes a marine colony. The parameters follow the sourced behaviour: call growl, call_m1/call_m2 = 10 and 3 for the October-March breeding season, food_tag invertebrate for the dominant prey, forage_gait walk and flee_gait hop for a hopping frog, night_lo_deg -90 and night_hi_deg -6 so it shelters only after dark, min_temp_c 12 and max_temp_c 30 for a frog active mainly when warm (the article gives narrower calling bands of 16-23 C in water and 14-25 C in air, which is the basis for gating calls on temperature), flee_m 3, calm_m 8 and freeze_m 6 as judgements for a large frog that freezes then hops away, and food_m 8 and water_m 25 for a terrestrial feeder that is never far from its breeding water.
